analysis_notes.source_text_structure: Torah LM2 #120 is a five-paragraph narrative teaching transmitted by Reb Nosson, reporting Rebbe Nachman's rebuke of a disciple who was praying with Lurianic kavvanot. The teaching's argument is: (1) Rebbe Nachman rebuked a disciple for praying with kavvanot and told him to focus only on the plain meaning of the words (פֵּרוּשׁ הַמִּלּוֹת כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ); (2) For one who is unworthy, praying with kavvanot is like kishuf (sorcery) — just as one may study sorcery to understand and rule on it but not practice it, so kavvanot may be studied to understand and teach but not used in prayer by the unworthy; (3) The essence of prayer is devekut (cleaving) to God — it would be better to pray in the vernacular since the heart naturally cleaves to words it understands, but since the Anshei Knesset HaGedolah established the Hebrew liturgy, one must use Lashon HaKodesh, and the main kavvanah is simply the plain meaning of the words; (4) One who speaks Lashon HaKodesh always (e.g., a Yerushalmi) need only attend to what he says — that is his kavvanah; (5) For the greatest true tzaddikim, all the Ari z"l's kavvanot are already subsumed within their plain-meaning understanding.
analysis_notes.bechina_language_scan: The word 'בְּחִינַת' does not appear anywhere in the source text. No equivalent bechina markers ('נקרא', 'כנ"ל' in an equivalence sense, 'הוא') are used to equate concepts. The comparison 'כְּמוֹ כִּשּׁוּף' (like sorcery) in paragraph 2 is a simile — it illustrates the severity of the problem by analogy, but does not assert that praying with kavvanot IS, in its essential nature, the same thing as sorcery. It is a rhetorical comparison (כְּמוֹ = like), not an identity statement (הוּא בְּחִינַת = is an aspect of).

key_concepts_identified.role_in_teaching: The Lurianic mystical intentions used in prayer. Rebbe Nachman forbids their use in prayer for those who are unworthy. All connections involving this concept in the teaching are eitza (cause-and-effect): using kavvanot (for the unworthy) produces a sorcery-like damage. No bechina equivalence stated.

The plain meaning of the prayer words. This is 'the essence of prayer' (עִקָּר הַתְּפִלָּה) — but the teaching uses 'עִקָּר' (essence/primary element), not 'בְּחִינַת' (aspect/parallel nature). The eitza chain is: intending the plain meaning → produces devekut → produces closeness to God. No bechina stated.
Cleaving to God. Described as 'the essence of prayer' (עִקָּר הַתְּפִלָּה). Produced by (eitza) focusing on the plain meaning. No bechina equivalence stated.

Sorcery/witchcraft. Used as an analogy for improper use of kavvanot — 'כְּמוֹ כִּשּׁוּף' (like sorcery). This is a simile, not a bechina. The Talmudic rule about sorcery ('לֹא תִלְמַד לַעֲשׂוֹת אֲבָל אַתָּה לָמֵד לְהָבִין וּלְהוֹרוֹת') is applied by analogy to kavvanot.

analysis_notes.conclusion: No gaps to fill. The source text contains no bechina statements, so there are no missing bechina edges to flag. All four key concepts (kavvanot, perush hamillot, devekut, kishuf) participate only in eitza (causal) or analogical structures. None are absent from the dataset in a way that creates a gap in bechina coverage, because there is no bechina coverage to be complete.
